title: Hurricane Nolo Is Crawling Toward Hawaii — And That's the Problem
summary:
What's scarier than a hurricane? A hurricane that won't leave.

Hurricane Nolo is moving toward Hawaii right now. Its winds are already 105 mph — that's a Category 2 storm. But here's the weird part: it's crawling at only 5 mph. That's slower than you ride a bike. Slow storms dump rain in one place for a long time, and that's exactly what forecasters fear.

Some areas could get more than 2 feet of rain. The National Hurricane Center says "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible." People on the Big Island are under a hurricane watch. Maui is under a tropical storm watch.

Nolo isn't expected to hit land directly. But it's still dangerous. Over the next three days, its winds could grow to 140 mph — a Category 4 storm.

This storm has been full of surprises. Earlier this week, forecasters said it was falling apart. Then it suddenly turned right, headed straight for Hawaii, and grew into a hurricane. Hawaii has already been hit hard this year: a huge flood in March, a 6.0 earthquake in May, and two other hurricanes. Governor Josh Green says about 1,290 homes have been damaged or destroyed.
why_it_matters: It shows how one slow storm can threaten thousands of families' homes and schools, and why weather warnings tell people to get ready long before the rain starts.

background_read: Hawaii is a group of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and it is the 50th state of the United States — far away from the mainland.
Hurricanes get their power from warm ocean water, which is why they often form in warm parts of the ocean and then move toward land.
Slow storms can be worse than fast ones: in 2017, Hurricane Harvey moved very slowly over Texas and dropped so much rain that whole neighborhoods flooded.
Article_Structure: WHO: Hurricane Nolo, forecasters at the National Hurricane Center, people on the Big Island and Maui, and Hawaii's governor, Josh Green.
WHAT: A slow-moving Category 2 hurricane is crawling toward Hawaii, with warnings about more than 2 feet of rain, dangerous flooding and mudslides.
WHERE: The Pacific Ocean near Hawaii — a hurricane watch for the Big Island and a tropical storm watch for Maui.
WHY: Because Nolo is creeping along at only 5 mph, it can dump rain on one place for days, and its winds may grow to 140 mph — a Category 4 storm.
